faqs.a: The shorthand takes up to four values in clockwise order starting at the top-left: top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left. With two values, the first applies to top-left and bottom-right, the second to top-right and bottom-left. One value rounds all four corners equally.
faqs.q: What order do the four border-radius values go in?

faqs.a: Percentages are relative to the element's own dimensions: horizontal radius is a percentage of the width, vertical radius a percentage of the height. That is why border-radius: 50% on a square makes a perfect circle, but on a rectangle makes an ellipse.

Yes, with the slash syntax: border-radius: 30px 10px / 10px 30px sets different horizontal and vertical radii, creating elliptical corners. This generator focuses on the common uniform-corner case, which covers the vast majority of designs.
faqs.q: Can corners be elliptical (different horizontal and vertical radii)?

faqs.a: Absolutely — border-radius works on images, videos, iframes, and any block element. For images, also add display: block or overflow handling if the image has its own background, and remember the corner clips the content, not just the border.

This usually happens when the radius is larger than half the element's smallest side — the browser scales all radii down proportionally so they do not overlap. Reduce the values or check that a percentage radius is not exceeding 50% of the box.
faqs.q: Why do my corners look different from what I typed?

faqs.a: Yes, overflow: hidden on the parent clips child content to the parent's rounded corners. This is the standard trick for cards with images that should follow the card's rounded shape.

keyFacts: The border-radius shorthand accepts one to four values, applied clockwise starting from the top-left corner.
Each corner can have an independent radius, which is how designers create blob shapes, leaf shapes, and asymmetric cards.
Pixel values give fixed corners that stay the same at any element size; percentage values scale with the element.
border-radius: 50% on a square element produces a perfect circle — the classic CSS avatar trick.
Corners also clip backgrounds, borders, and — with overflow: hidden — child content like images.
If the combined radii are larger than the element, the browser scales them down proportionally so corners never overlap.
